newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing shuns airshow limelight, Airbus flies high.
newsitem.headline: Boeing shuns airshow limelight, Airbus flies high.

text.p: Airbus Industrie has used this week's Paris air show to announce potential new aircraft sales worth some $3.5 billion, including a deal with Northwest Airlines Corp. announced Thursday -- in contrast with archrival Boeing Co., which has kept a low profile.
The four-nation European consortium said Northwest had signed a memorandum of understanding to order 50 A319 jets with options on up to 100 more.
The orders would be worth around $2 billion, based on an average price of $40 million per plane, representing the bulk of Airbus' air show announcements.

While past air shows in Britain and France have crackled with the competitive tension between Airbus and Boeing, there was a sense that this time around the Seattle-based company was not looking for a fight.

Industry executives here believe Boeing is being careful not to attract too much attention in Europe, while European Commission competition authorities probe its planned $14 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. A ruling is expected by the end of July.
Airbus's triumphant tone in its announcement Thursday was met with silence from Boeing, whose highly polished communications machine might normally have had a counterblast prepared.

Yet on close inspection the Airbus announcements embraced firm orders for just four planes worth up to an estimated $290 million, with the rest of the business consisting of commitments to buy -- but not firm orders.

At the last Paris air show two years ago, Boeing flew in its 777 giant twin-jet and announced it would make a "stretch" version of the plane. But all Boeing has shown off at this show so far is a niche product, the 737 Boeing business jet.

Industry analysts believe Boeing is concentrating on its merger with McDonnell Douglas. The merger would create a corporation with annual revenues of $48 billion, dwarfing Airbus, which had revenues of $8.8 billion in 1996.
Airbus argues the merger will create a market dominance aimed at eventually killing it off.
Boeing holds a share of around 60 percent of the world market, while Airbus has some 30 percent with McDonnell Douglas holding the rest.

Ron Woodard, the president of Boeing's Commercial Airplane Group, told reporters earlier this week that McDonnell Douglas sold three planes last year and held a 3 percent share of the market. "Douglas is in a declining position in the world market," he said.

Woodard also played down the importance of Boeing's exclusive supply deals with three U.S. airlines -- AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, Delta Air Lines Inc. and Continental Airlines Inc. -- saying the carriers themselves had asked for the sole-supplier terms.
With the world airline industry climbing strongly out of a deep recession in the early and mid-1990s, Boeing is pushing out aircraft as fast as it can to keep up with demand.

Boeing this year will build 40 planes a month, more than the previous record 39.5 in 1992, and will aim for 43 in 1998, Woodard said. The previous peak was just before a wave of order cancellations smashed through the industry.
Airbus Managing Director Jean Pierson earlier said the consortium partners will make modest investments to increase production facilities to handle more output.

Although the investment was small, the fact it was being made at all was significant, an Airbus spokesman said. The partners believed demand would be sustained rather than short-term, or they would have increased overtime work.

Airbus expects to deliver 185 aircraft this year and 220 in 1998. That compares with 126 last year. Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG; and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA of Spain.
